doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

chapter: Opinions on jazz and big bands
title: Why the big bands disappeared
summary: Television, the loss of radio remotes and dance halls, the war and Petrillo ended the big band era.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: What was your take on the reason the big bands really disappeared?

Well I think probably it was television for one thing, and just a lack of interest and I don’t know why really. We had all these dance halls that closed down all of a sudden. The radio, see the radio stopped. One of the big things about the big band era was the radio support. If you lived in this coast you could start about ten o’clock at night and turn on your radio and there’d be remotes from all over the world. And every band you can think of was on. And if you listened to — what the hell’s his name that does the yearly thing? Chuck Cecil? You ever heard of Chuck Cecil?

Well Chuck Cecil runs programs, the hits of ’48 and ’49 and so on. And he always opens by talking about these dance halls and we all know where they were. There was the Palladium in L.A. where Goodman broke through. There was Glen Island Casino over here and Frank Daly’s Meadowbrook, and Boston, everyplace. There were places all over the country that were known because they were broadcast from there. And that’s how these bands were made. That’s how Goodman was made. Goodman was made because of the broadcasts on the Camel Caravan. And that’s really what held it together. And these bands that traveled went from place to place and they had a built-in following. That all stopped. When the war came along it all stopped. Petrillo of course had his hand in it. He killed it for a while. And the people who continued and the ones who have continued to this day you can count on one finger practically. Les Brown. Welk. Welk’s no longer. That’s about it. They just aren’t. The Basie band without Basie, and all the ghost bands of course there are now. And they’re still making a living.
